data.title: Home heating oil price declines from October high but still up 59% YoY
data.description:
Key points:
  • The price per gallon of No. 2 home heating oil declined to $5.915 a gallon as of Nov. 9, the second weekly decline in a row, but still ~70% higher than the year-ago period.
  • Residential heating oil reached a 2026 high on Oct. 23 of $6.23, according to the US Energy Information Administration. Since the EIA began tracking home heating oil prices in October 1990, it has never reached that high. 
  • On Nov. 3, 2025, the price per gallon was $3.632. On Nov. 4, 2025, it was $3.486.
  • In October, the EIA predicted that consumers in the Northeast may not be as financially impacted as anticipated this winter as temperatures are not expected to be as cold as last year. That being said, the agency still predicts oil-heated homes could spend up to 21% more this winter on the fuel.

Telangana CM Revanth Reddy lays foundation and unveils campus master plan of PHFI Institute of Public Health Sciences
data.description:
Hyderabad, Nov. 14 -- Telangana Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy on Saturday assured that the state government would provide full support to entrepreneurs who come forward to invest in Telangana, emphasising that there is no 'policy paralysis' or confusion regarding state policies.

The Chief Minister stated that specific frameworks have been established to ensure the availability of land, water, necessary clearances, and infrastructure for investments.

According to a press release, while participating in laying the foundation and unveiling the campus master plan of PHFI Institute of Public Health Sciences today, the CM highlighted that the government's goal is to elevate the state to an international standard across the education, healthcare, industrial, and service sectors.

Institutions like the Indian School of Business (ISB) and NALSAR have played a pivotal role in gaining global recognition for Telangana and attracting significant investments to Hyderabad, CM Revanth Reddy said, expressing hope that organisations like the Public Health Foundation of India (PHFI) would contribute to establishing Hyderabad's international standing in the healthcare sector.

Stating that the TIMS hospital in Sanathnagar has already been inaugurated, and that other TIMS hospitals will also be made operational soon, the Chief Minister said that a new Osmania Hospital is being constructed in Goshamahal and a total of Rs 12,000 crore is being spent on the development of hospitals.

Domestic investors and the nations in the Middle East and Asia were looking toward Hyderabad for investment opportunities; the CM remarked that the visionary decisions made by past leaders laid the foundation for the development of present-day Hyderabad.

The CM further recalled that the country's literacy rate was only 12 per cent, and the population encountered severe hardships due to food shortages in the initial times of Independent India.

He added that the then-Prime Minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, prioritised the sectors of education and irrigation, and laid the foundations for prestigious institutions like IIT Kharagpur. The construction of projects such as Srisailam and Bhakra Nangal increased water availability for agriculture, enabling the country to transition from a state of food scarcity to one with a surplus of food grains.

Reddy also recalled that the technological shifts introduced by Rajiv Gandhi paved the way for the development of the information technology sector in the country. Many students who studied at the Hyderabad Public School are now excelling in high-ranking positions at prominent Fortune 500 companies globally.

The CM stressed that quality education should be provided amid increasing competition.

Chief Minister Revanth Reddy expressed his aspiration that even a student from a remote village in Telangana should rise to a level where they can compete with professionals working at the World Trade Centre in New York. The economic reforms introduced by PV Narasimha Rao provided a new direction for the nation.

Reiterating that his government continued to uphold the positive policies implemented by the previous administrations of Chandrababu Naidu, Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy, and KCR, the Chief Minister said that his government remains committed to continuing policies that foster development even despite political differences.

The CM highlighted that world-renowned universities are establishing centres in Hyderabad, making international-standard education accessible locally. The Chief Minister mentioned the creation of the "Telangana Rising 2047" vision, aimed at transforming Telangana into a developed state by 2047.

The Outer Ring Road (ORR) emerged as a great boon for Hyderabad, noting that approximately 13.4 million (1.34 crore) people reside within its periphery, the press release added. CM Revanth Reddy explained that industries located inside the ORR are being relocated while the area within is being developed into a hub for the service sector.

Furthermore, he highlighted the importance of the construction of a Regional Ring Road (RRR) outside the ORR, for which tenders have already been invited for a 160-kilometre stretch.

The goal is to develop the manufacturing sector across an area of approximately 10,000 square kilometres surrounding the Regional Ring Road. The government was inviting major global corporations to Telangana and providing all the necessary facilities for their investments, he said.

Stating that the 'Telangana Global Summit' will be held on December 7, 8, and 9, the Chief Minister noted that approximately 65 per cent of the state's revenue is generated from the areas surrounding Hyderabad and the Rangareddy district has the highest per capita income in the country.

The goal is to transform Telangana into a one-trillion-dollar economy by 2034 and a three-trillion-dollar economy by 2047. Efforts were also underway to increase Telangana's share of the national GDP to 10 per cent, he added.

The CM assured entrepreneurs that the state offers a favourable investment climate, encouraging them to invest with full confidence. The components for Rafale fighter jets are being manufactured within the GMR industrial zone in Hyderabad.

The Chief Minister said that the foundation for the state's pharmaceutical sector was laid in the 1960s with the establishment of IDPL, initiated by Jawaharlal Nehru and Indira Gandhi. Hyderabad has gained global recognition in the pharmaceutical sector by prioritising research and development; notably, 40 per cent of the country's bulk drug production takes place in the city.

According to a press release, the world-renowned pharmaceutical company, Eli Lilly, has come forward to invest one billion dollars in Hyderabad; the CM said that many international organisations were establishing Global Capability Centres in Hyderabad. The government was continuing the industrial policies introduced by previous administrations and remains committed to providing full support to investors.

Revanth Reddy emphasised that the government accorded the highest priority to the healthcare sector, noting that approximately Rs. 2,500 crore is spent annually through the 'Aarogyasri' scheme and the Chief Minister's Relief Fund.

The Chief Minister mentioned that cancer has been designated as a 'notified disease,' and data on patients across the state has been collected. Describing Telangana as a "data-rich state," the CM explained that analysing the information gathered through Aarogyasri can reveal the specific health challenges prevalent in different regions.

Expressing concern over the severe impact that fluoride issues and the pollution of the Musi River are having on the health of the people in Nalgonda district, the CM noted that it is also adversely affecting the health of unborn children.

Reddy stressed the urgent need to revive the Musi River, asserting that such purification is essential to safeguarding the health of the people of Nalgonda.

The Chief Minister set a target to complete the PHFI (Public Health Foundation of India) project by June 2, 2028, and assured that the government would provide comprehensive support for its establishment. The CM hoped that the PHFI would bring greater international recognition to Hyderabad and also announced that, in addition to providing the necessary support for the institution's development, he would personally serve as its brand ambassador.

data.title: Novo's Wegovy pill helps patients lose about 6% of weight in three months, real-world data show
data.description:
By Patrick Wingrove

Patients who stayed on Novo Nordisk's daily Wegovy pill lost an average of 6.2% of their body weight over three months, according to real-world data due to be presented at the ObesityWeek conference in Washington.

The pill, launched in January, has helped Novo regain some ground lost to Eli Lilly , and the Danish drugmaker is trying to stay ahead of its US rival in the race for oral obesity treatments.

Novo's Chief ​Scientific Officer Martin Holst Lange said in an interview that the real-world data was encouraging as it broadly replicated the findings of 5.5% weight loss at 12 weeks seen in Novo's late-stage trial for the pill.

Study participants, who started taking the pill between January 5 and February 7, 2026, lost an average of 6.3 kg (13.9 pounds) from a baseline weight of 103.0 kg (227 pounds), Novo said. About three-fifths lost at least 5% of their weight, and roughly one in six lost at least 10%.

The analysis covered 5,872 adults on the Ro telehealth platform who had never taken a weight-loss drug and who stayed on the pill for the full three months.

Novo Nordisk's fortunes have declined significantly since it became Europe's most valuable listed company following the 2021 launch of its injectable weight-loss drug, Wegovy. Its stock has plummeted over 70% from its peak as Lilly surpassed it to take the lead in the obesity-drug market.

According to company presentations earlier this month, however, oral treatments now represent roughly a third of US obesity prescriptions, with Novo securing over 80% of new oral prescriptions.

The company in September said separate real-world data showed patients who switched from weight-loss injections to Novo's pill continued to lose weight.

Oral Wegovy — known chemically as semaglutide — led to about a 14% reduction in body weight over 64 weeks, while Eli Lilly's obesity pill Foundayo led to about an 11% reduction over 72 weeks, separate studies have shown.

data.title: Strategy's Michael Saylor proposes $10B-$30B digital credit plan
data.description:
Strategy has spent years buying Bitcoin with two tools: selling new common shares and benefiting from a rising Bitcoin price. On its third-quarter 2026 earnings call, Executive Chairman Michael Saylor said the company may no longer need either one.

His pitch is that Strategy could create between $10 billion and $30 billion in what it calls "digital credit," backed by the balance sheet it already has. For a company whose whole identity is "buy more Bitcoin," that changes how the shopping gets funded.

Saylor described the $10 billion to $30 billion range as financing capacity. It would not require new common-stock issuance or any further gains in Bitcoin's price.

The $30 billion figure reflects the company's view of its own financial structure and Bitcoin holdings. It is not a fundraising target the company plans to hit immediately.

CEO Phong Le filled in the mechanics. He said the main way Strategy will acquire more Bitcoin going forward is by issuing preferred securities, particularly perpetual preferred shares such as STRC.

Perpetual preferred shares sit between bonds and common stock. Holders get a fixed dividend and stand ahead of common shareholders in line. They don't get voting power, and the shares have no maturity date. STRC is designed to pay double-digit yields and to work as a steadier alternative to holding Bitcoin directly.

As of October 25, 2026, Strategy held 848,517 BTC. That stack is up 26% for the year.

The company also reported about $5.07 billion in dollar assets. By Strategy's math, that reserve could cover preferred dividends and debt interest for roughly 3.4 years.

Strategy reported third-quarter net income of $19.53 billion, driven largely by a $20.91 billion gain on its digital assets.

Strategy already has a sizeable presence in this market. It currently has $16 billion in notional digital credit securities outstanding across ten listed instruments. The top end of Saylor's new range would be larger than everything it has issued in this category so far.

Strategy started as a traditional software company and has turned into one of the most prominent names among corporate Bitcoin treasuries.

The company now describes its capital approach in layers: digital capital, digital equity and digital credit. Bitcoin is the base layer. Common stock is the equity layer. The preferred instruments are the credit layer that the company now wants to lean on hardest.

The move also signals a step away from two funding sources that defined its earlier buying sprees: at-the-market (ATM) equity sales and convertible debt. ATM programs let a company sell shares into the market gradually. Preferred shares sidestep some of those issues. They don't add common shares, and perpetual instruments never come due. The trade-off is a standing dividend obligation that has to be paid regardless of where Bitcoin trades.

For common shareholders, the most obvious appeal is less dilution. If preferred issuance replaces ATM sales as the main funding channel, existing holders may see their ownership stretched less with each Bitcoin purchase. Their claim, however, sits behind a growing stack of preferred holders who get paid first.

For preferred buyers, the proposition is yield backed by a large Bitcoin position and a multi-year cash reserve. The 3.4-year coverage estimate is based on current obligations. Adding billions in new preferred paper would raise the annual dividend bill.

The reported earnings also deserve care from this group. A $19.53 billion quarter driven by a $20.91 billion digital-asset gain shows how directly Strategy's results follow Bitcoin.

data.title: Jensen Huang spy scandal puts Howard Lutnick in focus after Scott Bessent's remarks: What are his family's Nvidia ties?
data.description:
New Delhi, Nov. 14 -- US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has put Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick under fresh scrutiny over the Trump administration's handling of suspected Nvidia chip smuggling to China. Lutnick's family business ties to Nvidia and its AI partners have added another layer to the controversy.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's remarks about the handling of suspected Nvidia chip smuggling to China have brought Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick into the spotlight. Bessent said several government departments had supported placing Singapore-based Megaspeed on a restricted entity list for months, pointing to the Commerce Department as the agency responsible for taking action.

The comments have renewed attention on Lutnick's former Wall Street firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, which is now run by his sons, Brandon and Kyle Lutnick. The firm has reported investments in Nvidia and helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for companies connected to the chipmaker's artificial intelligence business.

There is no evidence that the family's business interests influenced Lutnick's government decisions or that his sons received confidential intelligence.

Before joining Donald Trump's administration in February 2025, Lutnick headed Cantor Fitzgerald. He later transferred his ownership stake to his children through trusts.

A CNBC analysis of securities filings found that Cantor's reported Nvidia shareholding fell by nearly 50% between September 2025 and March 2026.

At the end of 2024, the firm disclosed more than 3.5 million Nvidia shares worth approximately $479 million. Their value climbed to $652 million by September 2025. However, the reported share count fell to three million in December and 1.78 million by March 2026.

Cantor has not publicly explained the reduction. It has said the Nvidia positions reported in regulatory filings largely reflected client swap transactions rather than substantial standalone investments.

The controversy goes beyond Cantor's investments. According to Axios, Lutnick received a highly classified intelligence warning about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's alleged links to a suspected Chinese spy.

The Commerce Secretary also faced pressure from White House and intelligence officials to take action against Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of helping channel Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China.

Axios reported that Lutnick repeatedly resisted efforts to crack down on the company, despite Trump authorising fresh export restrictions.

Bessent's comments have exposed divisions within the administration over the issue. He said the Treasury, Defence and State departments, along with the US Trade Representative's office, had supported placing Megaspeed on the restricted entity list for months.

Cantor's business connections extend beyond its reported Nvidia shareholding.

In September, the firm hosted Huang and other senior Nvidia executives at investor meetings in New York. Its analysts subsequently maintained an overweight rating on Nvidia shares, describing the chipmaker as an attractive investment.

The firm has also helped finance companies in Nvidia's AI ecosystem.

In May 2026, Nvidia announced a five-year cloud computing agreement worth $3.4 billion with Australian company IREN. Days later, IREN announced a $3 billion convertible bond offering, with Cantor among seven banks arranging the deal.

Cantor also advised AI infrastructure developer Lancium on a $600 million financing deal for its data centre campus in Abilene, Texas. The project is connected to Stargate, the AI infrastructure initiative backed by OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle.

The overlap between Lutnick's government responsibilities and his family's financial connections has attracted attention from ethics experts and lawmakers.

Richard Painter, a former White House chief ethics lawyer under George W Bush, told CNBC there was no proof Lutnick had shared confidential information with Cantor Fitzgerald. However, he said the appearance of a potential conflict was concerning.

Democratic lawmakers have also called for greater scrutiny of whether the Lutnick family could benefit from the administration's AI infrastructure policies.

The White House continues to back Lutnick. An official told Reuters that Trump retains complete confidence in the Commerce Secretary.

So far, there is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of intelligence warnings about Huang or that Cantor's business interests influenced government decisions.

The Man Who Tells Corporate America How to Sell Stuff to Baby Boomers — WSJ
data.description:
By Rachel Louise Ensign | Photography by Ian Tuttle for WSJ

CHICAGO — Ken Dychtwald sat on stage in front of a ballroom of hundreds of people who work in the senior-housing industry.

Tan and fit in a black T-shirt and gray suit, he told the audience that their prospective residents will soon be the individualistic and high-maintenance baby boomers. "Get ready for the complaining," Dychtwald said to audience laughter. "Get ready for the demands."

Dychtwald has been predicting the ascendance of aging boomers for decades as a public speaker and boardroom consultant. Now the moment the 76-year-old has long forecast is here.

Selling things to older people was once an afterthought for companies. That has started to change in recent decades as the population aged. The boomer generation's massive size, high levels of wealth and desire to spend freely are making these customers even more desirable.

This generation collectively has far more money than any other group. According to the Federal Reserve, boomers currently hold more than $97 trillion in wealth, more than twice as much as the next-richest generation, Gen X. In the past year alone, boomers gained $12 trillion in wealth.

Dychtwald got his start in California's New Age scene. A fan of science fiction, he has tried predicting what the world would look like with the boomers as the most consequential group of older consumers yet. In a 1989 book, one of 19 he has written, he wrote that "the coming 'age wave' will challenge and shake every aspect of our personal, social and political dynamics."

Top executives started turning to Dychtwald for advice selling to the graying population. He advised Chrysler Chief Executive Lee Iacocca that the then-middle-age boomers would want to drive minivans. Dychtwald said he also played a role in the development of products including Michelob Ultra, multivitamin Centrum Silver, and Tylenol's arthritis product. He helped former President Jimmy Carter write a book.

Financial advisory firm Edward Jones hired Dychtwald in 2019. He worked with pollsters to survey thousands of people about retirement, finding that boomers increasingly saw retirement not as a time for rest but as a time for reinvention and exploration.

Dychtwald and Edward Jones dubbed their priorities — health, family, purpose and finances — the four "life pillars." The investment company trademarked the term, and its advisers now use the concept to guide conversations with their clients.

"It put words to something that they never had words for before," said Ken Cella, head of external affairs at Edward Jones. Dychtwald has done six more surveys for the company.

The Age Wave

Dychtwald grew up in a middle-class family in Newark, N.J., where his father owned area clothing stores. He left college, where he was studying to be an engineer, to move to California. He spent years regularly visiting the Esalen Institute in Big Sur, where nudity was common. Dychtwald got a Ph.D. in psychology and fashioned his dissertation on the mind-body connection as a book.

He started working with elderly people in his 20s when he helped run a program using yoga and meditation to improve their health. He eventually started his own company, Age Wave, to help companies understand the older demographic. Dychtwald learned about his subject by talking to older people and working with mentors including elderly-rights activist Maggie Kuhn. He once hired a professor to teach him about what it was like to be old throughout history.

In the 1990s, television network CBS was struggling to land advertisers because its viewers skewed older. They hired Dychtwald, who arranged meetings to persuade prospective advertisers these viewers were worth targeting. Those meetings yielded $600 million in new ad spending the following year, said Joe Abruzzese, who ran ad sales at CBS at the time. "He's probably the best speaker I've ever seen," Abruzzese said.

Dychtwald started building companies with products that catered to older people, such as local magazines and a health-products superstore. It gave him what he said was a net worth of more than $25 million. Those all unraveled right before the dot-com bubble burst, leaving him broke and contemplating suicide.

Eventually, he rebuilt his business. Now it has five employees, including his wife of 43 years, Maddy Dychtwald, who is also a speaker on aging.

'This Has Never Happened Before'

These days, Dychtwald spends much of his time doing interviews and giving speeches, where his going rate is $60,000. Two years ago, he addressed the Business Council, made up of CEOs of the largest U.S. companies. He does about half of his 15 or so keynote speeches a year now free to nonprofits.

Despite his decades in California, he retains an East Coast intensity. When audience members tell him they enjoyed his talk, he counters: "What about it was great?"

Talking about seniors is different now that Dychtwald is one himself. "I profoundly underestimated how painful it is to lose a loved one or how frightening it is to have your body start to fail," he said in an interview.

Both of his parents lived into their 90s, but with long declines — his mother had Alzheimer's disease and his father went blind from macular degeneration. Dychtwald estimates he spent around $1 million on home healthcare for them. Two of his friends died in recent months.

Dychtwald eats an anti-inflammatory diet, exercises twice a day, takes about a dozen different vitamins and gets regular massages. He has no plans to ever stop working.

He thinks companies are doing a much better job at catering to older Americans these days. High-end cruise lines are offering ambitious itineraries to curious older travelers. Home Depot hires elderly people for part-time jobs. Mercedes-Benz sells models that make it easier to get in and out, but doesn't pitch them explicitly to seniors. "They know their audience is older, but they don't hammer on it," he said. (These companies aren't currently clients).

Decades ago, Dychtwald predicted America would turn into a "gerontocracy," where economic and political power shifted from the young to the old. Dychtwald thinks politicians will start saying that boomers have too many resources. "We've made it really hard to be young," he said.

After decades of speeches, Dychtwald is closely attuned to his audience. At the October National Investment Center for Seniors Housing and Care conference, he asked people to raise a hand if they would like to live to 100. About half did, a likely testament to the group's familiarity with the dark side of growing old.

He called on audience members. "It's more about healthspan than lifespan," one said, referencing the buzzy idea that healthy years are what's most important. "Oh, there's great words," Dychtwald replied.

Dychtwald put up a slide with some stark demographic data. It showed the population of Americans 65 and over set to skyrocket, while all other age groups will grow slowly or even decrease. "Holy moly are you in the right places right now," he told the attendees about their line of work. "This has never happened before."

That compliment came with a grain of salt. Dychtwald suggested the industry might consider changing its name altogether. He showed a picture of Tom Cruise starring in the "Top Gun" sequel as an example of the new ideal. "I've looked at every study in the last 10 years. Boomers don't ever want to be a 'senior,'" he said. "I know that this is 'senior housing' and that worked. It may not work going forward."

data.title: Amylyx Pharmaceuticals Presents Results from Phase 3 LUCIDITY Clinical Trial of Avexitide in Post-Bariatric Hypoglycemia at ObesityWeek® 2026 Annual Meeting
data.description:
Amylyx Pharmaceuticals, Inc. () (“Amylyx” or the “Company”) will present the results from the 16-week double-blind treatment period of the Phase 3 LUCIDITY clinical trial of avexitide, an investigational, first-in-class glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor antagonist, in participants with post-bariatric hypoglycemia (PBH) following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) surgery, in a late-breaking oral presentation on November 15th at the ObesityWeek® 2026 Annual Meeting.

"The presentation of our Phase 3 LUCIDITY results represents a pivotal milestone in our work to address the longstanding treatment gap for people living with PBH. The results shared today reinforce the consistency and strength of the data, with avexitide demonstrating highly statistically significant and clinically meaningful reductions in hypoglycemic events across all prespecified endpoints,” said Camille L. Bedrosian, MD, Chief Medical Officer at Amylyx. “These positive data, together with positive results from five prior trials of avexitide in PBH, support the potential for avexitide to change practice for this debilitating condition.”

LUCIDITY met its prespecified primary endpoint, demonstrating a 55% reduction in the composite rate of self-monitoring of blood glucose (SMBG)-confirmed Level 2 and blinded Event Adjudication Committee (EAC)-adjudicated Level 3 hypoglycemic events compared with placebo (Least squares mean event rate of 0.55 events per week in avexitide arm compared to 1.24 events per week in placebo arm, p=0.0000034). LUCIDITY also met all prespecified, multiplicity-controlled secondary event-rate endpoints, reducing SMBG-confirmed Level 2 hypoglycemic events by 63% (p=0.0000032), EAC-adjudicated Level 3 hypoglycemic events by 47% (p=0.0016), and continuous glucose monitoring (CGM)-detected Level 2 hypoglycemic events by 42% (p=0.00016) compared with placebo. In a secondary analysis that evaluated change from baseline within each arm, events decreased by 72.9% in the avexitide arm and by 37.8% in the placebo arm (p=0.000034 for the between-arm difference).

Avexitide was generally well tolerated, with a safety profile consistent with that observed across prior PBH clinical trials. Treatment-emergent adverse events were primarily gastrointestinal and injection-site related and were generally mild to moderate in intensity. There were no deaths and no treatment-related serious adverse events. No clinically meaningful changes in body weight or fasting plasma glucose were observed during the 16-week double-blind treatment period.

“PBH is a chronic metabolic condition characterized by recurrent hypoglycemia. Each hypoglycemic event carries the potential for serious acute consequences and the cumulative burden of living with recurrent and unpredictable events can significantly affect daily functioning, independence, health and quality of life,” said Marilyn Tan, MD, FACE, FACP, Principal Investigator of the LUCIDITY clinical trial and Clinical Professor at the Stanford School of Medicine. “The debilitating nature of this condition is clear when you look at the participants of LUCIDITY. At baseline, the majority of participants entered the study experiencing daily hypoglycemia symptoms, with many reporting a history of loss of consciousness and hypoglycemia-related hospitalizations. This substantial disease burden makes the consistent reductions in hypoglycemic events seen with avexitide compelling.”

LUCIDITY is a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 3 clinical trial that enrolled 78 adults with PBH following RYBG surgery. After a 3-week run-in, participants were randomized 3:2 to avexitide 90mg subcutaneously once daily or placebo. Participants received standard-of-care dietary management for PBH throughout the run-in and 16-week double-blind treatment period. More than 90% of participants completed the double-blind treatment period, including 45/47 participants randomized to avexitide and 28/31 randomized to placebo. All eligible participants entered the 32-week open-label extension period. Baseline demographic and disease characteristics were generally balanced between groups. Participants in LUCIDITY had substantial disease burden at baseline: 68% reported daily hypoglycemic symptoms, 47% had a history of loss of consciousness, and 28% had a history of hypoglycemia-related hospitalizations.

"We're profoundly grateful to everyone who made LUCIDITY possible — from the people living with PBH who participated in our trial, to their families and care partners, as well as the investigators who share our commitment to improve outcomes for this serious condition," said Justin Klee and Joshua Cohen, Co-CEOs of Amylyx. "These results bring us meaningfully closer to what could be the first approved treatment for a community that has been waiting far too long for one. We're moving with urgency toward an NDA submission by year end and continue to prepare for a potential commercial launch of avexitide in 2027, if approved."

The FDA previously granted avexitide Breakthrough Therapy Designation for PBH. LUCIDITY’s 32-week open label extension period and the avexitide Expanded Access Program for eligible adults with PBH following RYGB surgery remain ongoing.

The ObesityWeek® 2026 Annual Meeting presentations can be accessed on the “Presentations” tab of the Amylyx website.

Webcast Information
Amylyx will host an investor key opinion leader (KOL) event tomorrow, November 15, at 11:45 AM ET both in-person and virtually to discuss the Phase 3 LUCIDITY results. A live webcast of the presentation and Q&A portion of the event can be accessed under “Events and Presentations” in the Investor section of the Company’s website, https://investors.amylyx.com/events-presentations. The webcast will be archived and available for replay for 90 days following the event.

About Avexitide
Avexitide is an investigational, first-in-class glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor antagonist that has been evaluated in six clinical trials for post-bariatric hypoglycemia (PBH) and has also been studied in congenital hyperinsulinism (HI). The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted avexitide Breakthrough Therapy Designation for both indications, Rare Pediatric Disease Designation in congenital HI, and Orphan Drug Designation for the treatment of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia (which includes PBH and congenital HI). In PBH, an exaggerated GLP-1 response leads to excessive insulin secretion, resulting in recurrent hypoglycemic events. Avexitide is a competitive GLP-1 receptor antagonist designed to bind to the GLP-1 receptor on pancreatic islet beta cells and inhibit the exaggerated GLP-1-driven insulin response characteristic of PBH, reducing inappropriate insulin secretion and stabilizing blood glucose levels. In two Phase 2 and the Phase 3 LUCIDITY clinical trials in PBH, avexitide demonstrated highly statistically significant reductions in hypoglycemic events.

About Post-Bariatric Hypoglycemia (PBH)
PBH is a chronic metabolic condition that is estimated to affect approximately 8% of people in the U.S. who have undergone the two most common types of bariatric surgery, sleeve gastrectomy and Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (approximately 160,000 people in the U.S.). PBH is thought to be driven by an exaggerated glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) response, primarily in response to food intake, leading to persistent, recurrent, and often debilitating rapid drops in blood glucose, known as hypoglycemia. The American Diabetes Association (ADA) recognizes hypoglycemia as a potential medical emergency because low blood glucose levels can compromise the body’s ability to maintain essential physiologic processes. In addition, hypoglycemia in the context of PBH may manifest as neuroglycopenia – an inadequate supply of glucose to the brain – which can cause confusion, cognitive dysfunction, loss of consciousness, and seizures. PBH can be associated with substantial disability, compromising safety, disrupting independent living, and affecting nutritional status and overall quality of life. Despite the substantial burden, there are currently no FDA-approved therapies for PBH.

data.title: Lilly says its obesity drugs helped patients lose weight in clinical trials

  • Zepbound reduced BMI by an average of 21.4% at 72 weeks in adolescents with obesity, with more than half no longer meeting the BMI criteria for obesity at 72 weeks.

  • Participants also reported improvements in weight-related quality of life, including physical comfort and body esteem, Lilly said.

data.title: L3Harris upgrade to communications system preceded ground stop: Duffy
data.description:
Friday's nationwide ground stop that led to the cancellations of thousands of flights into Saturday happened after an update was made to an older communications system used by air traffic controllers and managed by L3Harris Technologies .

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a Saturday morning news conference that the upgrade involved switching over from copper wires to a fiber network. "What we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router."

The router in question then started flooding other routers in the nation's air traffic control system with more than one thousand connection attempts every few seconds, Duffy noted.

"What that did is it gave us issues with communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruptions with our radar feeds."

At a Friday news conference, Duffy blamed the ground stop on outdated equipment, adding he would like some $50B to modernize the air traffic control system.

"President Trump has asked for the money," the secretary said Friday night. "He's asked the Congress on a bipartisan approach to say, 'Give us the resources to build a state-of-the-art air traffic control system.'" Let's not do a patchwork fix to a system that's critical for every single family. It's not red, it's not blue, it's not Democrat, it's not Republican, it's American. Give us the money to fix it."

data.title: India Inc flexes its strength in Q2
data.description:
India Inc’s Q2FY27 results point to strong revenue and profit growthdespite continued global upheaval, technological disruptions and supply chain volatility. Of the 2,864 companies that reported results till November 12, revenue and adjusted PAT (excluding extraordinary items) grew 23 per cent and 29 per cent year-on-year, respectively. Excluding the BFSI sector, growth rose to 26 per cent and 34 per cent, respectively.

Even after excluding refineries, where companies benefited from global shortages of diesel and other refined products, which boosted margins, revenue and adjusted PAT growth remained robust at 23 per cent and 25 per cent, respectively. Most major sectors contributed to the growth, while weakness elsewhere appeared largely transient, pointing to a strong quarter for corporate India.

Cost inflation, particularly in coal, power, logistics, steel and copper, was sharp during the quarter. Gross margins declined 257 basis points year-on-year in Q2FY27, an improvement over the 470-basis-point contraction in Q1FY27. However, strong volume growth improved operating leverage by spreading fixed costs, including employee, selling, general and administrative (SG&A) expenses and other overheads. This lifted EBITDA margins by 30 basis points, against a 215-basis-point contraction in the previous quarter.

Inflationary tailwinds were a net positive during the quarter. However, a sustained rise in prices could begin to affect demand, although this appears unlikely if tensions in West Asia ease.

As the table shows, steel, refineries and power delivered exceptionally strong performances among the major sectors. Banks, financial services and automobiles also reported robust growth, while most other sectors performed reasonably well.

Exceptional growth

Interestingly, both steel and cement, which rank at the top and bottom of the sector table, respectively, benefited from strong volume growth and higher realisations while facing rising input costs. However, steel performed significantly better, with stronger price and volume growth than cement. Steel prices rose 12-15 per cent year-on-year, compared with a 1-5 per cent increase in cement prices.

Higher coking coal costs affected both sectors, but operating leverage benefited steel companies more than cement makers. Within cement, industry leader UltraTech reported revenue and PAT growth of 19 per cent and 22 per cent, respectively. Other players recorded lower realisation growth and gained less from operating leverage, while higher input costs weighed on sector performance.

Refineries recovered from an 80 per cent year-on-year decline in PAT in Q1 to a 60 per cent increase in Q2. Significantly higher refining margins more than offset losses on oil and LPG distribution, which were lower than expected at State-run companies. Refining margins could contract in Q3 following the decline in crude oil prices. However, over the medium term of one to two years, margins could remain higher than in previous years as some refining capacity in Russia and West Asia has been impaired.

Power generation companies benefited from strong demand and improved realisations, with higher coal costs passed on through merchant power contracts. Although coal costs pressured margins, higher capacity utilisation and operating leverage, reflected in healthy plant load factors, cushioned the impact.

Capacity expansion plans at companies such as Adani Power and NTPC point to expectations of a sustained demand-supply gap. Capital goods, an allied sector, also benefited. Orders for gas, thermal and nuclear power projects, along with data centre demand, are driving growth.

Strong performers

Banks reported strong growth in credit and improvements in asset quality, while the cost of funds remained mixed. The outlook is also positive, with SBI expecting loan growth of 14-15 per cent and healthy net interest margins (NIMs) in FY27.

FCNR deposits supported NIM expansion at some banks, including SBI and PNB, while HDFC Bank and ICICI Bank reported marginal contractions. Forex swap costs and a sharp surge in liquidity also affected performance. These pressures are expected to ease as liquidity conditions normalise, reducing banks’ need to raise funds at a time when interest rates are expected to rise.

Overall, higher liquidity and fund availability could benefit banks in the near term.

For NBFCs, disbursements remained strong across categories, particularly in gold loans. Bajaj Finance, for instance, reported 100 per cent year-on-year growth in this segment. The momentum is expected to sustain across categories. However, early signs of the impact of El Nino on rural, agricultural and tractor financing are emerging, as highlighted by Shriram Finance in its quarterly update. This warrants monitoring across FMCG, rural banking, agriculture and housing. A rate-hike cycle could also compress NBFCs’ interest margins, while individual underwriting capabilities will ultimately determine their performance.

GST cuts announced last year improved affordability, while an extended festive season boosted automobile sales. Maruti Suzuki and Mahindra & Mahindra (M&M) reported 25 per cent year-on-year growth in passenger vehicle volumes. Electric vehicle and export performance was also strong. However, margins contracted as steel, copper and rubber prices rose, with price hikes only partially offsetting the higher costs.

The outlook for automobile demand remains positive, with M&M and Bajaj Auto reiterating their expansion plans. However, tractor sales, which are more exposed to agricultural conditions, could remain sluggish, as M&M has flagged.

Slower growth

The IT sector continued to face headwinds, with a weak outlook persisting. Infosys lowered its FY27 guidance, citing pricing pressure. AI-related projects now account for 10 per cent of revenues at both TCS and Infosys. However, revenue deflation as clients use AI to optimise costs continues to weigh on growth. A recovery will depend on clients moving from AI-led cost optimisation to using the technology to gain a competitive edge. The industry has yet to reach that stage.

The FMCG sector recorded healthy volume and price growth across both urban and rural markets, although the impact of El Nino could become visible in the next quarter. Margins narrowed as raw material, packaging and logistics costs remained elevated. Companies are likely to pass on these costs through calibrated price increases.

Pharmaceutical companies reported normalised revenue growth of 16 per cent year-on-year, but earnings were hit by largely one-off costs across the sector. Sun Pharma, Torrent Pharmaceuticals and Alkem Laboratories incurred acquisition-related expenses. Lupin, Cipla and Dr Reddy’s Laboratories were affected by product performance in the US market and launch timelines.

Contract development and manufacturing organisation (CDMO) companies were the bright spot, with Divi’s Laboratories and Laurus Labs reporting strong growth in both revenue and profit, reinforcing the sector’s ongoing upcycle.

data.title: AI Agents Can Now Buy Computing With Bitcoin—Does Lightning Have Its Use Case?
data.description:
AI agents have a new way to spend Bitcoin: buying the computing needed to keep working. Lightning Labs has launched pi402, a tool that lets coding agents pay for AI inference over the Lightning Network.

The November 12 announcement moves the agent-payments debate toward a specific purchase. Rather than imagining software shopping autonomously for everything, it starts with a recurring need: access to an AI model that can process the next prompt.

“Inference is the fuel every agent runs on,” Lightning Labs’ Olaoluwa Osuntokun wrote. The business question is whether a Bitcoin payment can make that fuel easier to buy and sell.

How AI agents use Bitcoin for inference

Pi402 connects the Pi coding-agent environment with paid inference services. The launch describes an embedded Wavelength wallet and controls for per-request spending and daily budgets. A human still funds the wallet and sets the operating boundaries.

The attraction is access without creating a separate buyer account or supplying a card to each participating seller. That does not make the entire AI service anonymous, unregulated or free of provider conditions. It changes the payment and access mechanism for services that implement it.

According to the L402 documentation, a buyer first requests a protected resource. The server returns a payment-required response, a credential and a Lightning invoice. Paying produces proof that can be presented with the credential to gain access.

The payment becomes part of authorisation rather than an invoice to settle later. The documentation also describes restricting and delegating bearer credentials, which matters when one piece of software needs to give another a limited ability to buy or access resources.

The useful detail is metering, not a payment for every word

The Aperture v0.6.0 release notes describe prepaid bundles that are drawn down according to actual usage. A single Lightning payment can therefore support multiple model requests. The system does not need to initiate a separate payment for every generated token.

The proxy obtains a price, reserves an estimated amount for a request and accounts for the reported usage afterward. When the remaining balance cannot cover another request, it can issue a new payment challenge.

That distinction separates a plausible billing system from a flashy demonstration. Model responses vary in length. Sellers need a way to price that uncertainty, and buyers need to see what they have actually consumed.

The same release supports both L402 and the Payment HTTP Authentication Scheme used by the Machine Payments Protocol. Supporting more than one payment-authentication format could help services meet different clients, although compatibility by itself does not establish commercial adoption.

The seller still has costs, accounts and exchange-rate exposure

Lightning Labs’ public Lightmeter repository shows another important layer. It converts a provider’s dollar-denominated model prices into millisatoshis per token, can add a seller margin and reconciles usage against the provider’s billing records.

A millisatoshi is one-thousandth of a satoshi. That granularity allows small accounting units, but the conversion does not make the underlying computing free or ensure that Bitcoin-denominated prices stay constant.

The repository’s architecture places the upstream provider’s API key at the proxy. In other words, removing an API key from the buyer’s experience does not necessarily remove API keys from the supply chain. Someone still needs to secure the provider relationship and pay its bill.

That gives the story a more grounded commercial angle. A reseller could offer a narrow, paid entry point to computing while managing procurement and billing behind it. Whether that arrangement is attractive depends on price, reliability, model access and the terms of the upstream service.

Why irreversible payments are a trade-off

Osuntokun argues that card chargebacks are poorly matched to computing that has already been consumed. A completed response cannot be ungenerated so that a seller can recover the electricity and GPU time.

Final payment can reduce that particular uncertainty for a seller. For a buyer, however, it raises the importance of spending controls and service quality. Paying successfully establishes access; it does not prove that an answer is correct or that an autonomous workflow was worth its cost.

BNC’s coverage of Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2 examined falling model prices alongside the continuing need for human judgment. Automating payment makes that distinction more consequential: a system can spend efficiently while pursuing an unhelpful task.

The adoption test starts with something measurable

The launch supplies software and an identifiable use case, rather than evidence that a large new market already exists. The announcement does not establish independent transaction volume, recurring demand or a broad network of competing sellers.

Useful follow-up evidence would include repeat purchases, the number of active providers, total payment costs and how often spending limits prevent unwanted work. Those measures would help distinguish a convenient developer tool from a meaningful new source of Lightning usage.

For Bitcoin, the opportunity is straightforward: a machine-native service being bought through a machine-readable payment. Pi402 makes that proposition testable. Its success will depend on whether developers keep choosing it after the novelty of an agent with a wallet has worn off.

data.title: Indonesia seeks to preserve historic railway assets as part of global heritage
data.description:
Semarang, Indonesia, Nov 14, 2026 - (ACN Newswire) - Indonesia's historic railway infrastructure represents an important part of global transportation heritage that must be preserved while adapting to modern development, according to an Indonesian architecture expert.

Ikaputra, a professor of architecture at Gadjah Mada University (UGM), said Java's railway system reflects the evolution of transportation technology and its influence on urban development, economic activity, and social transformation.

Speaking at the "Heritage Reimagined" architecture seminar during Rail Heritage Forum 2026 in Semarang, Central Java, Indonesia on November 9, he emphasized that Indonesia's railway infrastructure should be recognized as both a national historical asset and part of global railway heritage.

Indonesia's railway history dates back to 1867, when construction of the country's first railway line began in Central Java.

According to Ikaputra, railway heritage includes historic stations, tracks, engineering technologies, and operational facilities that have shaped communities for generations.

He stressed that conservation efforts must protect the historical and architectural significance of these assets while allowing them to remain relevant to contemporary society.

Meanwhile, President Director of state railway operator PT Kereta Api Indonesia (KAI) Bobby Rasyidin reaffirmed the company's commitment to preserving its extensive historical assets alongside modernizing railway operations.

"Beyond managing extensive railway assets, KAI also carries a rich historical legacy. That is why we are focused not only on railway operations but also on protecting and preserving our numerous cultural heritage sites," Bobby said.

He noted that railways played an important role in Indonesia's history, including supporting transportation during the country's struggle for independence.

Bobby also revealed plans to revive historic mining railway routes in West Sumatra, connecting Padang Panjang, Singkarak, and Sawahlunto, as part of the company's heritage preservation efforts.

"In West Sumatra, God willing, we will revive the historic mining railway routes, from Padang Panjang and Singkarak to Sawahlunto," he said.

"To shape the future, we must never forget where we came from," Bobby added.

Organized by KAI under the theme "1867 & Beyond: Preserving the Past, Shaping the Future," Rail Heritage Forum 2026 brought together academics, heritage experts, and railway stakeholders to explore ways to safeguard Indonesia's railway history for future generations.

data.title: Boston Fed's Collins Backs Gradual Rate Increases as Inflation Broadens — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Megan Leonhardt

Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins is on board with more higher interest rates, but she's a fan of a gradual approach — further piling on to expectations that a December rate increase is a lock and strengthening the case for 2027 hikes.

"I would currently see a steady, gradual approach as potentially being appropriate in this context," Collins said when speaking with reporters on Saturday during the Boston Fed's annual economic conference, which focused on the housing market. "The price data we've seen over the past three months, and the labor market on a stronger footing, does make me think that the path of policy, of rates, over the next year might be a bit higher than I had thought a couple of months ago."

But Collins, who is not currently a voting member of the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee, said that given the continued geopolitical and economic uncertainty, the exact path will need to be decided meeting by meeting as data becomes available. She said she believes that a "gradual path is the better way to stitch through" the persistent risks.

"I think the direction for monetary policy is clear, I don't want to get out ahead of how quickly it makes sense to move or how much to move rates," Collins said.

Collins defended the Fed's slow approach so far to raising rates. The central bank tightened monetary policy by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.75% to 4.00% in September, but kept rates steady in October. There's ongoing uncertainty that officials must weigh, Collins said. It is plausible, for example, that the rise in medium- and longer-term rates since the beginning of the year may actually weigh on demand more than expected or that enthusiasm around artificial intelligence investment wanes and creates economic shocks, Collins said. In those scenarios, there may be a greater risk to the economy associated with an aggressive rate hiking cycle.

On inflation, Collins said that she's carefully watching the data to see if price pressures related to the recent shocks, for example, in energy, are broadening out. The October consumer price index reading, which was hotter than expected, did show much broader pressures. Prices on everyday things, from groceries to home furnishings to medical services, experienced large increases last month. Even when excluding the effects of the oil shock and volatile food prices, core inflation translated into an annual growth rate of 2.8%, up from September's 2.6% pace.

Tariffs are also still a factor Collins is monitoring. Goods price inflation, for example, had been deflationary, but that component has risen a bit. In September, good inflation was up 0.7% year-over-year.

Inflation has been elevated for a long time, Collins acknowledged, saying that the Fed needs to follow up on its commitment to bring inflation back down to 2%. She said "some further tightening of monetary policy is appropriate."

Looking at employment conditions, Collins said she's less concerned. The "unusual stability" of the labor market has prevailed, she said, adding that it's "on somewhat more solid footing." While there's been less dynamism in the labor market in recent years due to a lower supply of available workers, she sees it largely in balance — and said that there is the potential for more growth than the U.S. has experienced so far over the past two years.

The fact that hiring has broadened across sectors is also giving her some comfort. Up until recently, month job growth was heavily concentrated in healthcare and social assistance, a situation that made labor conditions more vulnerable to shocks.

The recent strength of the labor market — payrolls gained 165,000 and unemployment ticked down to 4.1% in October — may be a sign of things to come. Collins said that she's hearing from employers in her district that companies are looking to hire.

"It's an unusual labor market, in my view. But what I see is stability and, somewhat more strength — with the potential that we could see more tightening," Collins said.

Commercial vehicles (CV) major Ashok Leyland Ltd reported an 8.7 per cent increase in consolidated net profit at ₹891 crore for the second quarter ended September 2026 as against ₹820 crore in the same quarter last year.

Consolidated revenue from operations rose 35 per cent and stood at ₹17,030 crore in Q2 FY27.

On a standalone basis, net profit rose 13 per cent to ₹869 crore. Revenue grew 39 per cent to ₹13,364 crore.

data.title: What's Fueling the Real-Estate Frenzy ?Taking Over Palm Beach This Week — WSJ
data.description:
By E.B. Solomont

A $75 million teardown. A compound trading hands for $84 million. A renovated estate asking $100 million.

Those were just three of this week's real-estate listings and deals in Palm Beach, Fla. On the affluent barrier island, the uber-wealthy have been gobbling up property since Covid and never really stopped. But as a real-estate reporter for The Wall Street Journal, covering three major properties in as many days was a lot, so I set out to find out what's behind the frenzy.

"The Season" has started

The peak social season in Palm Beach typically runs from late fall to early spring, so the uber-wealthy are in town and making real-estate moves. Meanwhile, deals that went into contract months ago are now closing in time for the season. "You have to be looking in August, September, October to enjoy it by November," said Margit Brandt of Premier Estate Properties, who recently represented Netscape co-founder Jim Clark in his purchase of a waterfront compound for $84 million, plus furniture and art, for almost $100 million in total. "The waterfront here is what's really moving," Brandt said.

Art Basel is coming, and so are the billionaires

Local agents said the flurry of big listings is also driven in part by the upcoming Art Basel art fair in December. While it takes place in Miami Beach, Palm Beach agents said there will be an influx of wealth into South Florida for the event around that time.

The midterm elections could be another potential factor behind the recent market activity, according to Carmen D'Angelo Jr. of Premier Estate Properties, who said some high-net worth individuals feel targeted by political rhetoric on the left and see Palm Beach as a safe haven.

Deals above $50 million have normalized

Several top agents said they are having the best years of their career, surpassing the heady days of 2021 and 2022. At least eight homes have sold for $50 million or more so far this year, compared with six last year, according to public records and data analysis by The Wall Street Journal.

Eight- and nine-figure prices are no longer surprising, said Gary Pohrer of Serhant, who is representing the buyer of a $40 million compound set to close in December. "The buyer asked, 'Am I overpaying?'" he said. "I said you're paying more than it's technically worth, but I can't find you another one."

Inventory is nonexistent

The number of single-family homes for sale in Palm Beach is down about 30% compared with last year, said Dana Koch of the Corcoran Group, who said inventory has been "persistently low" since Covid. "We don't have many ready, willing and able sellers."

Land prices are soaring

Scarce inventory is driving up land prices. Developer Todd Michael Glaser and a partner recently went into contract to buy a home on roughly 2 acres for $160 million — though later backed out over fears a neighbor could block development. Koch recently listed a potential teardown on the Intracoastal Waterway for $75 million.

Home prices are up — by a lot

The ultra high-end market is driving the market in Palm Beach. The median sale price was $12 million during the third quarter, up 20% from $9.9 million in the same period of last year. Turnkey properties command a premium, Brandt said. "People want to have immediate use."

She cited a continued influx of interest from buyers in California, Washington and New York. "Florida has welcomed wealth," she said. "Anybody that can afford to be in Palm Beach wants to be."

  • Additional reporting by Katherine Clarke

data.title: How I Used AI to Make My Grandson a Children's Book for Less Than $200 — WSJ
data.description:
By Ken Wells

Parents and grandparents who make up stories for their children and grandchildren often think: "I would love to turn this into an illustrated book."

And then they check into costs and learn that illustrating a 32-page book by a top-notch artist can run up to $20,000 — and that doesn't include printing.

If you have that kind of money, or if you think your book has commercial potential, by all means hire an illustrator. But now there is another way for hobbyists: Artificial-intelligence programs, among them Adobe's Firefly, Neolemon, OpenArt and ChatGPT, that are all capable of creating first-rate, suitable-for-printing images.

I know firsthand that illustrators are expensive, because two years ago I paid an artist $3,600 to draw a dozen illustrations for a self-published children's Christmas book inspired by, and featuring likenesses of, my first two grandchildren. For my next children's book, a surprise birthday present for my third grandchild, Sawyer, I decided to test AI instead.

Sawyer turns one in December, so anything I produced would have to be colorful, bright and short to keep his attention. And it would be full of illustrations that looked like him and his parents.

I came up with a fantastical story involving a loon and a lone boy, and gave it the title "Little Sawyer's Giant Adventures," with this beginning:

Sawyer would come each year with his parents to his grandparents' cabin on a pond in Maine.

He was little, but he dreamed big.

He dreamed of a giant moose named Marvin.

He dreamed of a giant beaver named Bucky.

He dreamed of a giant loon named Louie.

The program I used, Firefly, is included in my $70-a-month Adobe software subscription. For that, I get 6,000 credits a month toward creating high-resolution illustrations, at 300 credits per image.

Like Adobe, most of these programs let you experiment with creating lo-res images free, but you'll need a subscription to do the kind of heavy lifting involved in my project, generating 23 hi-resolution illustrations. For ordinary consumers, subscriptions run from as little as $10 a month to the $70 a month I pay. If you run out of credits, providers are thrilled to sell you more.

Firefly and other AI models operate on plain word prompts typed into a dialogue box. You also must choose the size of the illustration and its resolution — in other words, how crisp and detailed it looks. I burned up 3,600 credits — and had to start over — before I settled on the specs that worked best. So, that is lesson No. 1: Plan ahead.

To create the images, I uploaded pictures of that I wanted Firefly to use as references for the illustrations: one of our log cabin; a headshot of Sawyer; and a picture of his parents. Firefly — well, most of the time — will put those reference pictures in the image at the place of your choosing and dress them to your liking.

I instructed Firefly to give me an image for an "illustrated children's book" using the cabin and the pond as the backdrops. Further, I typed, "Have the boy standing on the pond bank while his parents are watching from the cabin porch. Dress them all in summery hiking clothes." Firefly blew me away on two tries by coming up with this:

It was the look, feel and personalization I wanted. Of course, it wasn't literal (or perfect). Firefly aged Sawyer into a toddler. The pond could be mistaken for a river. And, in the picture, his parents are the same height when, in fact, his mom is taller — something quite clear in the reference image I'd sent. I asked Firefly to fix it, but on three tries the image came back unchanged. Nine hundred credits wasted; cue the annoyance.

Telling Firefly to keep the style it had created, I asked it to put the boy in successive scenes in which he is dreaming of a giant moose, then a giant beaver, then a giant loon. They came back as instructed, but with no variation: Sawyer is in the same sleeping position in the same room, decor unchanged, in each frame.

I had also erred. There was nothing in the dream bubbles to show that the critters were giants. Since Louie the Loon was the vehicle for Sawyer's adventure, I asked Firefly to keep the image it had produced but put the loon next to a tiny red speedboat for perspective. And, oh, add a stuffed giraffe and loon to Sawyer's bedside to add variety to the decor. Bingo: It produced this image:

I then had Firefly remake the giant moose and giant beaver images similarly. Lesson No. 2: Be specific in what you want. (And now you can see how easy it is to burn through credits.)

After dreaming of Louie, Sawyer is out paddling with his parents in a kayak when they see an ordinary-looking loon. Sawyer knows it is the Louie of his dreams and tells his parents so as he waves to the loon and calls out his name. And, of course, the loon is Louie, who is lonesome and has a secret: At night, he becomes a giant who avoids other loons because he fears they will be jealous of his transformation. He's glad Sawyer waved to him and shows up at the cabin dock that night for a visit.

Using the dream scene above as the reference image, I asked Firefly to create an image of Sawyer coming out to meet Louie on the dock. The first try was good — except that Sawyer comes out wearing a life vest. I asked Firefly to keep the image but delete the life jacket. Perfect:

Sawyer convinces the loon to take him on a flying journey. I asked Firefly to show Louie offering Sawyer — wearing a "flying hat" and a life vest for good measure — his wing. My prompt was long and complicated, but Firefly delivered:

At my prompting, Firefly then created a beautiful image of Sawyer and Louie taking off, which I placed on the page under large text reading: "A giant loon can go wherever it wants to go." That was a setup for a series of silly images in which they visit, among others, the Man in the Moon, and see "astronauts trying to eat spaghetti." I laughed out loud when Firefly produced this in about two minutes:

Firefly was also able to create an alluring cover and back cover — something that saved me a few hundred dollars if I'd hired a professional (although I did have to purchase 2,000 extra credits for an additional $11.49 to complete that). The self-publishing site I used, BookBaby, charged $99 to print the 32-page book and ship me a proof copy.

The process requires patience and planning, and there is a learning curve that might be intimidating to the techno-challenged. And the glitches I described weren't the only ones. More than once, Firefly mysteriously injected text or captions into images. For a scene involving Sawyer in the kayak with his parents, Firefly put the kayak on the pond bank.

Still, all in all I was thrilled with the results — and am on to my next project.

Write to reports@wsj.com. You can read a PDF of "Little Sawyer's Giant Adventures" with all of the illustrations on Ken Wells's website at bayoubro.com.

data.title: Travel Woes Persist as Airlines Race to Reset After Groundstop — WSJ
data.description:
By Joseph Pisani

The groundstop is over but the pain at the airport isn't.

Nearly 3,900 flights were canceled and more than 2,300 were delayed on Saturday, a day after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide for four hours because of technical issues.

"Operations are slowly returning to normal," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday in a social-media post. "You will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most."

Friday's schedule disruptions left planes and crew members out of place for their next flights, and undoing the chaos caused by the groundstop is expected to take days.

At New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport on Saturday, flights were canceled minutes before boarding was supposed to start, with announcers citing staffing issues. Airlines, including United, Delta and American, said they would waive ticket-change fees. Airports encouraged people to check their flight status to avoid long wait times.

Duffy blamed the groundstop on old technology, and he used a press conference at the White House on Friday to plead with Congress to approve funding to upgrade the country's air-traffic system, an overhaul he said would cost $50 billion. Without it, he said outages could happen again.

"We have old switches, old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines," he said at that news conference. "It's an old system that went down."

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters that there wasn't any indication that the outage resulted from a cyberattack, but didn't rule it out.

Mullin attributed the outage to "putting patches into the system" and said that new equipment and technology overwhelmed the older system.

After the groundstop lifted about 8:15 p.m. ET on Friday, a group of travelers inside Terminal C at New York's LaGuardia Airport thought they were lucky: Their flight to Minneapolis was the last in the terminal that hadn't been canceled, and a gate agent said the plane and crew were ready to go.

Then, a new gate agent approached with the bad news: Like so many others, Flight 2349 had been canceled, too.
